Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 48, verse 4–10:

The hostility of the polytheists toward them, in preventing them from the House (the Ka'bah), had become severe, to the point that "Umar said: 'Why should we accept humiliation in our religion?' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'I am the servant of God and His Messenger; I will not disobey His command, and He will not abandon me.'" Then God caused contentment with what had happened to settle in the hearts of the Muslims, and so they submitted and obeyed.

﴿That they might increase in faith﴾: whenever a duty was revealed, their faith increased.

﴿And to God belong the hosts of the heavens and the earth﴾: He means that all the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth belong to Him. Had He willed to support His Prophet by other than you, He would have done so, but He chose you for this, so thank Him.

So this verse was revealed," related by Anas ibn Malik. Muqatil said: when 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy heard of that, he set out with a group of men to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "What is for us with God?" So the verse was revealed: ﴿and punish the hypocrite men. . .﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir said: the lam in "li-yudkhila" is repeated upon the lam in "li-yaghfira," so the meaning is: "Indeed We have granted you a victory, that God may forgive you, that He may admit the believing men," and for this reason no conjunction waw was placed between them; the meaning is: "that He may admit and that He may punish."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 48, verse 15:

What follows this is clear, up to His words: ﴿Those who were left behind will say﴾, namely those who stayed behind from al-Hudaybiyah, ﴿when you set out to take spoils﴾. The reason is that when they (the Prophet and his companions) turned back from al-Hudaybiyah with the treaty of peace, Allah promised them the conquest of Khaybar, and it was specified for those who witnessed al-Hudaybiyah. So they set out toward it, and these who had stayed behind said: ﴿Let us follow you﴾. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They wish to change the words of Allah﴾. And Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "an yubaddilu kalima Allah" (to change the words of Allah) with a kasra on the lam.

There are two opinions regarding the meaning.

The first: it refers to Allah's promises of the spoils of Khaybar to the People of al-Hudaybiyah specifically. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is Allah's command to His Prophet that none of them should march with him. This is because Allah had promised him, while he was at al-Hudaybiyah, that He would give him Khaybar, and forbade him that any of those who had stayed behind should march with him. This is the view of Muqatil.

According to both opinions, they intended that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) should permit them what contradicts the command of Allah, which would be a changing of His command.

His words, the Exalted: ﴿Thus has Allah said before﴾ contain two opinions.

The first: He said that the spoils of Khaybar are for those who witnessed al-Hudaybiyah, and this is according to the first opinion.

The second: He said, "You will never follow us." This is the view of Muqatil.

﴿Rather, they will say, you envy us﴾, meaning: envy prevents you from our sharing the spoils with you.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 48, verse 16–17:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You will be called to a people﴾. The meaning: if you desire raiding and booty, then you will be called to fight a people ﴿possessing great might﴾.

Regarding these people there are six opinions.

The first: they are Persia. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, 'Ata' al-Khurasani, Ibn Abi Layla, and Ibn Jurayj, among others, said the same. The second: Persia and the Romans, said by al-Hasan, and narrated by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid. The third: they are the people of idols, narrated by Layth from Mujahid. The fourth: they are the Romans, said by Ka'b. The fifth: they are Hawazin and Ghatafan, and that was on the day of Hunayn, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatada. The sixth: the Banu Hanifa on the day of al-Yamama, who were the companions of Musaylima the Liar, said by al-Zuhri, Ibn al-Sa'ib, and Muqatil. Muqatil said: the caliphate of Abu Bakr in this is a clear and emphatic proof. (p-432) Rafi' ibn Khadij said: "We used to recite this verse and did not know who they were, until Abu Bakr was called to fight the Banu Hanifa, and then we knew that they were them." Some of the scholars said: this verse cannot be about anyone other than the Arabs, due to His saying, ﴿you will fight them or they will submit﴾, whereas Persia and the Romans are only fought until they submit or pay the jizya. Bukayr ibn al-Ashajj said: "The tree was in a mountain pass towards Makkah." Nafi' said: "The people used to come to that tree and pray beside it. As for His words after this: ﴿Allah has promised you abundant spoils that you will take﴾, the exegetes said: these are the conquests that will be opened to the Muslims until the Day of Resurrection.

The first: they were the Jews who intended to ambush the dependents of the Muslims whom they had left behind in Madinah, but Allah restrained them from that. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: He increases your guidance through believing in Muhammad (ﷺ) in what he brought from Allah's promise of conquest and spoils.

The fourth: because of the scarcity of water in it.

The second: He increases your guidance through believing in Muhammad (ﷺ) in what he brought from Allah's promise of conquest and spoils.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 48, verses 27–28:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah has certainly fulfilled for His Messenger the vision in truth﴾. The exegetes said: the occasion of its revelation was that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had been shown in a dream, before his departure to al-Hudaybiyah, a speaker saying to him: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾, up to his saying: ﴿without fear﴾. He saw that he and his companions were entering Makkah, having shaved their heads and trimmed their hair. He informed his companions of this, and they rejoiced. When they set out for al-Hudaybiyah, they supposed that they would enter Makkah in that same year. When they returned and had not entered, the hypocrites said: "Where is his vision that he saw?!" Then this verse was revealed, and they entered in the following year.

Regarding His saying: ﴿if Allah wills﴾, there are six opinions.

The first: that "in" (inna) means "when" (idh). This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: that it is an exception made by Allah, though He knows (the outcome), and people make exceptions regarding what they do not know. This was said by Tha'lab. According to this, the meaning is that He knew they would enter it, but He made the exception in accordance with what He commanded creation to do regarding exception.

The third: that the meaning is: "You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque if Allah commands you to," said by al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: that the exception refers to the entry of some of them or all of them, because He knew that some of them would die; related by al-Mawardi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 48, verses 27–28:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah has certainly fulfilled for His Messenger the vision in truth﴾. The exegetes said: the occasion of its revelation was that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had been shown in a dream, before his departure to al-Hudaybiyah, a speaker saying to him: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾, up to his saying: ﴿without fear﴾. He saw that he and his companions were entering Makkah, having shaved their heads and trimmed their hair. He informed his companions of this, and they rejoiced. When they set out for al-Hudaybiyah, they supposed that they would enter Makkah in that same year. When they returned and had not entered, the hypocrites said: "Where is his vision that he saw?!" Then this verse was revealed, and they entered in the following year.

(p-443)

Regarding His saying: ﴿if Allah wills﴾, there are six opinions.

The first: that "in" (inna) means "when" (idh). This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: that it is an exception made by Allah, though He knows (the outcome), and people make exceptions regarding what they do not know. This was said by Tha'lab. According to this, the meaning is that He knew they would enter it, but He made the exception in accordance with what He commanded creation to do regarding exception.

The third: that the meaning is: "You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque if Allah commands you to," said by al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 48, verse 29:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah﴾. Al-Sha'bi, Abu Raja', Abu al-Mutawakkil and al-Jahdari read: "Muhammadan Rasula Allah" with the accusative in both. Ibn Abbas said: [Allah] bore witness to him as a Messenger.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who are with him﴾, meaning his companions. Al-ashidda' (the stern ones) is the plural of shadid (stern). Al-Zajjaj said: The original form is ashdida', like nasib and ansiba'; but since the two dal's became vowelled, the first was assimilated into the second, [and similar to it is] ﴿whoever of you turns back﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 54].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Merciful among themselves﴾. Al-ruhama' is the plural of rahim (merciful). The meaning is that they are harsh toward the disbelievers and affectionate among themselves. ﴿You see them bowing and prostrating﴾ describes the abundance of their prayer (p-446) ﴿seeking bounty from Allah﴾, which is Paradise, ﴿and approval﴾, which is Allah's pleasure with them. This description applies to all the Companions according to the majority. Mubarak ibn Fadala narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri that he said: "Those who are with him" — Abu Bakr; "stern toward the disbelievers" — Umar; "merciful among themselves" — Uthman; "you see them bowing and prostrating" — Ali ibn Abi Talib; "seeking bounty from Allah and approval" — Talha, al-Zubayr, Abd al-Rahman, Sa'd, Sa'id and Abu Ubayda.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Their mark﴾, i.e., their sign, ﴿is in their faces﴾. Is this sign in this world or in the Hereafter? There are two opinions.

One: it is in this world. Then there are three sayings.

The first: it is good bearing (samt hasan). Ibn Abbas said this in the narration of Ibn Abi Talha; and in the narration of Mujahid he said: Indeed it is not what you think, but it is the mark of Islam, its bearing and its humility. Likewise Mujahid said: It is not the dust-smudge on the face, but it is humility, gravity and modesty.

The second: it is the moisture of purification and the dampness of the earth; this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Abu al-Aliya said: Because they prostrate on the dust, not on garments. Al-Awza'i said: It reached me that their foreheads never bore anything from the earth [without its mark].

(p-447) The third: it is the scorching of the sun; when a man's face is scorched by the night, he becomes yellowish in the morning. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "Their mark in their faces": the yellowness. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the trace of wakefulness. Shamir ibn Atiyya said: it is an agitation in the face from night vigil.

The second opinion: it is in the Hereafter. Then there are two sayings.

One: the places of prostration on their faces will be the brightest of their faces on the Day of Resurrection; this was said by Atiyya al-Awfi, and al-Hasan and al-Zuhri went in a similar direction. Al-Awfi narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: Their prayer will appear on their faces on the Day of Resurrection.

The second: they will be raised with bright white marks from the trace of purification; al-Zajjaj mentioned this.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is their likeness﴾, i.e., their description; the meaning is that the description of Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions ﴿in the Torah﴾ is this.

As for His saying: ﴿And their likeness in the Gospel﴾, there are three sayings.

(p-448) One: this likeness mentioned as being in the Torah is their likeness in the Gospel. Mujahid said: Their likeness in the Torah and the Gospel is one.

The second: the preceding is their likeness in the Torah; as for their likeness in the Gospel, it is His saying: ﴿like a seed﴾. This is the saying of al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd.

The third: their likeness in the Torah and the Gospel is "like a seed." Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi mentioned these sayings.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It sends out its shoot﴾. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Amir read ["shatahu" with fatha on the ta' and hamza]. Nafi', Asim, Abu Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "shatespecially" with sukun on the ta' ("shat'ahu"). All of them read it with a fatha on the hamza. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu al-Aliya and Ibn Abi Abla read: "shata'ahu" with fatha on the ta', [with madd] and hamza, and with an alif. Abu Ubayda said: that is, its offshoots; it is said: "ash'ta al-zar'u" (the crop sent out shoots), so it is mush'it when it has put forth shoots. ﴿Then it strengthens it﴾, i.e., it made it equal, and it became like the mother [plant]. Ibn Amir read: "fa'azarahu" with a short hamza, like fa'alahu. Ibn Qutayba said: azara means he helped it and strengthened it. ﴿So it grows thick﴾, i.e., it became thick. ﴿And stands firm on its stalk﴾; the word is the plural of "saq" (stalk). This is a parable which Allah, mighty and majestic, struck for the Prophet ﷺ when he went out alone, then He strengthened him with his Companions, just as the shoot of the crop strengthens the stalk with what grows from it until it becomes large, thick and firm. Ibn Kathir read "ala suw'qihi" with hamza; the rest without hamza. Qatada said: In the Gospel: a people will come forth who grow as a crop grows.

(p-449) Concerning who is meant by this parable there are two sayings.

One: the root of the crop is Abd al-Muttalib; ﴿it sends out its shoot﴾: it sent out Muhammad ﷺ; ﴿then it strengthens it﴾: with Abu Bakr; ﴿then it grows thick﴾: with Umar; ﴿and stands firm﴾: with Uthman; ﴿on its stalk﴾: Ali ibn Abi Talib. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated this from Ibn Abbas.

The second: the crop refers to Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿it sends out its shoot﴾ is Abu Bakr; ﴿then it strengthens it﴾ is with Umar; ﴿then it grows thick﴾ is with Uthman; ﴿and stands firm on its stalk﴾ is with Ali. ﴿It pleases the sowers﴾: meaning the believers; ﴿that He may enrage the disbelievers by them﴾. This is the saying of Umar to the people of Makkah: "Allah will not be worshipped in secret after today." Al-Dahhak narrated it from Ibn Abbas, and Mubarak from al-Hasan.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That He may enrage the disbelievers by them﴾, i.e., He only multiplied and strengthened them so that He might enrage the disbelievers by them. Malik ibn Anas said: Whoever rises in the morning with rage in his heart against the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, this verse has afflicted him. Ibn Idris said: I am not sure that they have not come to resemble the disbelievers, meaning the Rafidah, because Allah, exalted is He, says: "That He may enrage the disbelievers by them."

(p-450) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah has promised those among them who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: Regarding "min" (among/from) there are two views.

One: it is for specifying the kind, distinguishing it from others, like His saying: ﴿So avoid the filth of the idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30]. A similar usage is when you say: "Spend from the dirhams," meaning: make your spending of this kind. Ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning of the verse is: Allah has promised those who believe from this kind, i.e., from the kind of the Companions.

The second: this promise is for those among them who persist in faith and righteous deeds.
